ev.eur_fc_baptism.midwife.ok: The midwife poured warm water over your head three times: "I baptise thee in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." A week later the priest only had to read the remaining prayers over you.
ev.eur_fc_baptism.church.ok: You were bundled in a sheepskin and carried through the cold to the church. The priest baptised you at the stone font, your godparents named you, and at home it was a long time before you warmed up.
ev.eur_fc_baptism.priest: Fetch the priest to the house
ev.eur_fc_baptism.priest.ok: Your father ran for the priest and slipped him a coin for his trouble. You were baptised by the hearth in a tub of warmed water — not quite proper, but warm.
ev.eur_fc_baptism.title: Baptise at once
ev.eur_fc_baptism.text: You were born in the night, a feeble little thing, barely breathing. The parish church is a long way off, and if a child dies unbaptised it cannot lie in consecrated ground. The midwife says she can baptise you herself, right now: the Church allows it when a life is in danger. Or you could be wrapped up warmly and carried to the priest.
ev.eur_fc_baptism.note: The Church taught that an unbaptised infant could not enter heaven or lie in the churchyard, so children were baptised within days, even hours, of birth. If a baby was weak, the midwife or any Christian could baptise it; synods required midwives to know the words of the sacrament. If the child lived, the priest later completed the rite in church.
ev.eur_fc_baptism_midwife.title: The midwife
ev.eur_fc_baptism_midwife.text: The old midwife who baptised you the night you were born calls you "my little christening child" and keeps feeding you honey cakes. You follow her about the district carrying her basket, and already know which herb is for fever and which for colic.
ev.eur_fc_baptism_godparent.title: Your godparent
ev.eur_fc_baptism_godparent.text: The {g:godfather|godmother} who once held you over that cold font called you over: "You're grown, and I've done nothing for you yet." {g:He|She} taught you a little of {g:his|her} trade, put in a word where it mattered, and gave you a silver coin at parting.
ev.eur_fc_balia.village.ok: You were taken off to the village in a cart, in a basket of straw. For two years you grew up among hens, goats and other people's children, and came home brown as a nut, with a country accent.
ev.eur_fc_balia.home: Take a nurse into the house
ev.eur_fc_balia.home.ok: The nurse moved into a little room next to the nursery. She sang you village songs and never let you out of her sight, and your mother, though jealous, was at ease.
ev.eur_fc_balia.mother.ok: Your mother nursed you herself. The aunts shook their heads, while the preacher at church praised it: so nature and Scripture command.
ev.eur_fc_balia.title: A wet nurse from the village
ev.eur_fc_balia.text: In a good house a baby is given to a wet nurse, and your father has already found a young peasant woman from a village outside the town: she will take you home for a year or two and asks very little. You could have a nurse live in instead — dearer, but the child stays under your eye. Your mother wants to nurse you herself, though the family grumbles that it isn't done.
ev.eur_fc_balia.note: Well-off townsfolk and nobles often gave their babies to wet nurses. Florentine fathers recorded in their household books what they paid the peasant balia and how much cloth and soap they sent her; in Paris a royal ordinance of 1350 fixed nurses' wages and regulated the agencies that hired them. Preachers, meanwhile, urged mothers to nurse their own children.
ev.eur_fc_balia_flour.title: A sack of flour
ev.eur_fc_balia_flour.text: In a hungry winter a cart drew up at your house: the husband of your old wet nurse had brought a sack of flour and dried apples. "My wife said our milk-child mustn't go hungry." You barely recognised him, but he looked at you as if you were still lying in that basket of straw.
ev.eur_fc_balia_tales.title: The nurse's tales
ev.eur_fc_balia_tales.text: Your nurse stayed on in the house — as your nanny now. In the evenings she tells you about werewolves, saints and crafty peasants who trick their lords, and you fall asleep holding on to her apron. Nobody in the house knows you better.
